author: Stephen Jordan
headline: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
text: Daily briefing, 2026-11-04, compiled Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:44 UTC. The story: Researchers have developed an AI-native experimental laboratory called AutoDNA for autonomous biomolecular operations, according to a study published in Nature on November 4, 2026. The system was created by a team including researchers with ORCID identifiers and authors such as Jiabin Wang, Zhiyuan Dong, Jingkai Yang, Qingting Li and Tianyu Huang. AutoDNA is designed to carry out multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments with minimal human intervention. The work was published as an article in Nature with supporting data, code and supplementary information. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to perform core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing. Human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields and accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold. It also completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. The authors say AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing applications in synthetic biology and information storage. They describe the system as realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework through co-design of models, experiments and instruments. The paper frames the work as addressing a long-standing goal of AI-native laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention. The authors note that existing autonomous experimental systems remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. The study positions AutoDNA against an add-on architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than giving it a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. The data supporting the findings are available in the article and its supplementary information, with sequencing data and agent-related outputs available at Zenodo. The code is available on GitHub, and the version used in the study is also available at Zenodo. Reference genome hg38 was downloaded from the National Center for Biotechnology Information, and further data are available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request.
